text: Καὶ μόνος καὶ ἀπαθής. Id certe, quod ad meritum ac nutum attinet divinæ charitatis: quam tamen, quod pro præsenti statu non ita habemus, ut sibi omnes motus nostros plene subjiciat, nondum ipse in se conspecto summo Bono et universali, nec sibi duntaxat, sed et nobis, infinito; hinc est ut nostra omnis ἀπάθεια, ac quam vel Maximus, vel alii Orthodoxi celebrant, veræ illius quam exspectamus, perfecta cum Deo unitione, jamque adulta et in termino charitate, quædam inchoatio sit, non ipsa vere ἀναμαρτησία, qua quasi a nobis, vique status; et nisi Dei auxilio, nedum peccare non possimus, sed et omnino possimus non peccare; quidquid tandem senserint, quos eo nomine Hieronymus Origenianos monachos exagitat, duriusque Theophilus insectatus est; a cujus excessu, quiescentibus illis motibus, visa magis per Ægypti Nitriæque deserta vigere Christiana nostra ἀπάθεια, quam illa Christi gratiæ invia et Stoica.
anchorLine: καὶ μόνος καὶ ἀπαθής (a), τῇ πρὸς τὸ ἐν ἀσχέτῳ νεύσει γενό-
en: (a) 'Both alone and impassible.' This is certainly so as regards the merit and inclination of divine charity; but since in our present state we do not have it in such a way that it fully subjects all our motions to itself (the highest and universal Good not yet being beheld in itself, and infinite not only for itself but for us), it follows that all our impassibility, which Maximus and other Orthodox celebrate, is only a kind of beginning of that true impassibility we await, with perfect union with God and charity now full-grown; it is not truly sinlessness itself, [...] and unless by God's help we cannot merely avoid sinning but can altogether not sin; whatever those whom Jerome in this connection harries as Origenist monks may have thought, and whom Theophilus pursued still more harshly; after whose excess, their motions being quieted, the Christian impassibility of ours seemed rather to flourish through the deserts of Egypt and Nitria, than that inaccessible and Stoic one of Christ's grace.

text: Μὴ ἀνθρώπων ἀπειλή. Indicant hæc omnia Georgii animum curis ancipitem, Constantinopolim profectum, quo forte evocabatur ad diluendam suspicionem, et unde resilierit, cum non sibi tutum satis putaret ab æmulis. Haud certe facile viro principi ut non obnitatur, nedum amittendæ dignitatis, sed et mortis ipsi discrimini.
en: (b) 'Not of men the threat.' All this shows Georgius's mind to have been anxious with cares, having gone to Constantinople, where perhaps he was summoned to dispel a suspicion, and (it shows) why he drew back, since he did not think himself safe enough from his rivals. It is certainly not easy for a man to refuse to resist a prince, still less when loss of rank, and even danger of death, is at stake for him.

text: Καὶ στυγνότητα πτήξεως. Hanc Veneti codicis lectionem merito præfero, quod ea sensus expeditus, nec sic dicta πτῆξις a carceris infernalis pœna abhorreat. Nam τὸ πτήσσειν, proprie dici volunt de animantibus, quæ conspecto hoste prodire non audent, sed præ metu in loco aliquo apto ad latitandum se contrahunt. Habet et vim quamdam cessandi, quod qui metu comprimuntur, nec movere se, nec mussitare audent. Sic itaque in inferni barathro pavidi semper reprobi, quæ illis tristitia maxima et mœror. Τὸ πήξεως, communius est, magisque respiciat inanima; nec tam στυγνότητα legendum, quam στενότητα: ut fixæ tartari angustiis morae injucunditas designaretur; quod voluisse videbatur Dufrenii Antiquarius in illa voce parum depravata, στεγνότητα, non explicato motu proprio viventium, ex mali imminentis cum stupore certa exspectatione.
anchorLine: … ἀφανισθέντα ... στυγνότητα πτήξεως (c), τῶν ἐκουσίων ἡμῶν κακῶν
en: (c) 'And the gloominess of cowering.' I rightly prefer this reading of the Venetian codex, because it gives a clear sense, and the word so used (πτῆξις) is not repugnant to the punishment of the prison of hell. For τὸ πτήσσειν, they say, is properly said of animals which, seeing the enemy, dare not come out but through fear crouch down in some suitable place to hide. It also has a certain force of ceasing, since those held down by fear dare neither move nor mutter. So in the pit of hell the reprobate are ever fearful, and theirs is the greatest sadness and grief. [The word] πήξεως is more general and looks rather to inanimate things; and στυγνότητα should not be read so much as στενότητα, so that the unpleasantness of delay in the narrow straits of fixed Tartarus would be indicated; which Dufresne's Antiquarius seemed to intend in that somewhat corrupt word στεγνότητα, without explaining the proper movement of living things, from the sure expectation of imminent evil with stupor.

en: Neither ruling nor being subject, neither living in the opulence of riches nor oppressed by poverty, is a matter of will and mind's judgment; it belongs rather to Providence, which governs all things.

text: Extrema vocat ortum et interitum; medium vero ortus et interitus, ipsum est quod oritur, in quo plerumque interitus ortum occupat, rem, cum necdum orta sit, interitione delens.
en: He calls the extremes birth and destruction; but the middle of birth and destruction is that very thing which comes to be, in which destruction often forestalls birth, wiping out the thing before it has yet been born.

text: Qui sensuum libidini animum defixum habent, tametsi iis vacent affectibus atque vitiis, quæ sensus oblectant, haud tamen, inquit, salutem consequentur, quin perfecte ab ea in sensus libidine animum avocaverint; uti nec beatus Lot, nisi Sodomis exiisset, etsi non patrabat Sodomitarum nefanda, ignis de cœlo missi pœnam evasisset.
en: Those who keep their mind fixed on the pleasure of the senses, even if they are free of the passions and vices that delight the senses, will not, he says, attain salvation unless they have wholly called the mind away from the sensual pleasure; just as blessed Lot, had he not left Sodom, though he did not commit the abominations of the Sodomites, would not have escaped the punishment of the fire sent from heaven.

en: Those who have the soul nailed to attachment to the senses are not saved, he says, even if they are idle as to the passions that please the senses, unless they remove the soul entirely from attachment to the senses; just as not even blessed Lot, had he not gone out of Sodom, even though he did not do the deeds of the Sodomites, would have escaped the descent of the fire.

text: [continuation of note (d) begun at the foot of p-0214, in the NOTÆ block of this page]: que præsidio. Quod sic absolute cubicularius dicitur, princeps videatur eorum, qui a sacro cubiculo erant, isque forsitan qui rem privatam curabat, ac quem communius παρακοιμώμενον Græci scriptores vocant: qui et quandoque vir integer erat. In hac de charitate epistola, vere maximum agit Maximus, ac nescio an divinius majorique emphasi de charitate ab ullo scribi possit, cujus vel maxime mysterium, non hic solum, verum etiam aliis passim locis vir sanctus mirifice detexit; ut qui alte animo eam imbibisset, Deique in ejus præcepto ac lege scopum apprime exploratum haberet; qui ipse totius dispensationis ac mysterii Christi scopus est: ut unum cum Deo, aliique cum aliis simus, vicissimque curemus ac curemur: quod ipsum in præcepto eleemosynæ, sequenti ad eumdem epistola, contemplatur.
anchorLine: Τοῦ αὐτοῦ πρὸς Ἰωάννην κουβικουλάριον (d), περὶ ἀγάπης. (on p-0214)
en: [...] [faith]ful protection. That he is called simply 'cubicularius' suggests the chief of those who were of the sacred bedchamber, and perhaps the one who managed the private property, and whom Greek writers more commonly call παρακοιμώμενος; who was also at times an upright man. In this letter on charity Maximus truly treats of the greatest thing, and I doubt whether anything could be written about charity more divinely or with greater emphasis, whose mystery above all the holy man has marvelously disclosed, not only here but elsewhere throughout; as one who had drunk it deep into his mind and had the aim of God's precept and law thoroughly tested; who himself is the aim of the whole dispensation and mystery of Christ: that we may be one with God, and with one another, and in turn care for and be cared for; which same thing he contemplates, in the commandment of almsgiving, in the following letter to the same man.
remark: Joins the note (d) printed on p-0214; the NOTÆ block here is the second part of that same note, set in two columns under the page. The word 'cubicularius' (not κυβικουλάριον) opening this page's Greek cites is part of the continuing text.
